newsitem.title: ITALY: Food summit chief blasts world over Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: Food summit chief blasts world over Zaire crisis.

text.p: The head of the U.N.'s Food and Agriculture Organisation, Jacques Diouf of Senegal, accused the world on Monday of doing nothing to prevent the crisis in Zaire, saying it had been clear a catastrophe was in the making.

In a strong critique of past inaction, Diouf said the international community had allowed the problem of refugees from Rwanda and Burundi to "fester" to the point where more than a million are now at risk from the violence in eastern Zaire.
He said the crisis would figure on the margins of FAO's World Food Summit, which opens in Rome on Wednesday, but defended the meeting for focusing instead on a global plan to combat hunger.
"We believe that this situation (in Zaire) is another illustration of an unacceptable world situation," Diouf, the agency's Senegalese director general, told a news conference to present the summit.

"But at the same time it is a lesson for us all in so far as this situation shows that when you leave a situation to fester, when you wait until you are in a crisis, the solutions to the problem become more difficult and more expensive," he said.

Diouf said it had been clear that refugees in camps in Zaire, set up when they fled ethnic slaughter in Rwanda and Burundi, had been "under the yoke" of Hutu rebels he said had been responsible for genocide.
"Nothing was done about it," Diouf said, saying the same inaction had characterised the international response to conflicts in Bosnia and Somalia.
"We risk having similar situations elsewhere unless we respect a certain number of principles and unless we act in anticipation to avoid such situations," Diouf said.
He declined to identify potential crisis countries but said FAO, which groups 174 members, had made its concerns about other flashpoints known to national governments.
"We hope that they will listen more on those than they did on the Great Lakes situation," in central Africa, Diouf said.

The World Food Summit, first proposed by Diouf, is set to adopt a plan of action that will commit governments to working to eradicate hunger, with an immediate aim of halving the number of undernourished people by 2015 from the present 840 million.

Several African heads of state, including presidents Daniel Arap Moi of Kenya and Benjamin Mkapa of Tanzania, are due to attend the five-day gathering, making unofficial contacts on the Zaire crisis a likelihood.
But Diouf said in response to a question that FAO was the wrong agency and the summit the wrong forum to address the human catastrophe, given the military and political implications.
"The FAO will not substitute for what is happening in New York," at the U.N. Security Council, Diouf said.
"An event tragic as it is, and this one is tragic, should not also make us lose sight of the fact that there are people who are dying quietly not under the cameras of the TVs of the world.
"I would like this summit to take care of that problem and not only for the present but for the future to avoid that in the future we face this type of crisis," he said.

Diouf again said that some 100 heads of state and government would attend the five-day summit but that FAO would not release names until "we get all the information about the arrival of the world leaders".
He also defended the gathering from critics who say the world has had enough of summits after a string of major U.N. conferences on global problems in the past two years.
"If you tell me another way by which I can get the people of the world to get together to take decisions regarding the future of humanity, I am ready to consider it," Diouf said.
